idiom_name: private final lock object with synchronized blocks
implementation_notes: Java gives every object an intrinsic lock, but using the guarded object's own monitor is Monitor Object; the guardian form is a private lock instance - `private final Object lock = new Object()`, or a private `ReentrantLock` - that no other class can acquire, with every field private and every operation written as a synchronized block on that lock. The tutorial's `MsLunch` example builds two such objects 'solely to provide locks', one per field group, which is also the pattern's limit: the lock object is what gives the guardian its monopoly, so synchronizing on `this`, on a `Class` object or on an interned string re-opens it to outside interference and deadlock. The Java memory model supplies the visibility guarantee (monitor exit happens-before the next monitor enter), so guarded reads and writes cannot be reordered out of the critical section, but nothing prevents publishing the state from inside an operation.
pitfalls: Synchronizing on `this`, on a `Class` object or on an interned string hands the lock to every caller; the lock object must be private, final and used for nothing else.

Returning the guarded collection (or its iterator/spliterator) lets callers traverse and mutate it outside the monitor - a failure mode Java's own `Collections.synchronizedX` wrappers document for iteration.

Holding the monitor across a callback or a blocking call serialises the whole application behind the guardian and invites re-entrant deadlock; intrinsic locks are reentrant, which hides the design error rather than preventing it.

variants.name: Private ReentrantLock (with conditions) as the guardian
variants.idiom_name: private final ReentrantLock lock, try/finally lock/unlock
variants.implementation_notes: Replacing the intrinsic monitor with a private `ReentrantLock` keeps the guardian idea and adds what `synchronized` cannot express: `tryLock` with a timeout to refuse instead of waiting, interruptible acquisition, an optional fairness policy, and `Condition` objects for guarded waiting (the tutorial's `Safelock` example uses a per-object `ReentrantLock` exactly this way). The price is that the release is manual, so every guarded operation needs a `try/finally` - a leaked unlock turns the guardian into a deadlock. On Java 21+ there is a second reason to prefer it: a virtual thread that blocks inside `synchronized` pins its carrier thread, while `ReentrantLock` parks without pinning.
pitfalls: `lock()` without a `finally { unlock(); }` leaks the lock on any exception path, and the guardian never recovers.
Switching to `ReentrantLock` does not make callbacks safe: the critical section is still serialised, and `Condition.await()` must only be called while holding the lock.
